title: Global Aridity Index and Potential Evapotranspiration (ET0) Climate Database v2
abstract:
The Global Aridity Index (Global-Aridity_ET0) and Global Reference Evapotranspiration (Global-ET0) Version 2 dataset provides high-resolution (30 arc-seconds) global raster climate data for the 1970-2000 period, related to evapotranspiration processes and rainfall deficit for potential vegetative growth, based upon the implementation of a Penman Monteith Evapotranspiration equation for reference crop. The dataset follows the development and is based upon the WorldClim 2.0: http://worldclim.org/version2
Aridity Index represent the ratio between precipitation and ET0, thus rainfall over vegetation water demand (aggregated on annual basis). Under this formulation, Aridity Index values increase for more humid conditions, and decrease with more arid conditions. The Aridity Index values reported within the Global Aridity Index_ET0 geodataset have been multiplied by a factor of 10,000 to derive and distribute the data as integers (with 4 decimal accuracy). This multiplier has been used to increase the precision of the variable values without using decimals.
The Global-Aridity_ET0 and Global-ET0 datasets are provided for non-commercial use in standard GeoTiff format, at 30 arc seconds or ~ 1km at the equator.

narrative:
Short impact summary

The Global Aridity Index and Potential Evapotranspiration (ET0) Climate Database v2 has become a widely used reference dataset for climate, hydrology, and dryland research. The record shows 333 scholarly citations, 405 documented downstream reuses, and 1,233 downloads, alongside evidence of use across high-profile journals and a broad international research community.

Full narrative

This 2019 Figshare dataset by Antonio Trabucco and Robert J. Zomer provides high-resolution global climate rasters for aridity and reference evapotranspiration over the 1970–2000 period. Its impact is strongest as infrastructure: it functions as a reusable environmental baseline that other researchers draw on for analyses of aridification, vegetation dynamics, hydrology, species distributions, and climate response.

The citation record indicates sustained scholarly uptake, with 333 citations concentrated in recent years and a steady stream of reuse across article, preprint, peer-review, and book-chapter literature. The dataset is cited in venues that include bioRxiv, Global Change Biology, New Phytologist, Nature Communications, Nature Ecology & Evolution, Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, and Biogeosciences, suggesting that it is embedded in work with substantial visibility across ecology, earth system science, and biogeography.

The reuse profile reinforces that role. OpenAlex and related records show 405 downstream works making use of the dataset, and the surrounding concept profile is centered on hydrology and watershed management, plant water relations and carbon dynamics, ecology and vegetation studies, species distribution under climate change, and climate variability and models. That pattern is consistent with a foundational dataset that supports both process-based and spatial modeling.

Usage and stewardship signals also point to durable accessibility. Figshare reports 5,297 views and 1,233 downloads, and the dataset is openly available with versioned DOI infrastructure and prior-version relationships preserved. Public-discourse data are sparse in this record, and scite shows one supporting citation statement, so the clearest evidence of influence comes from scholarly citation, reuse, and download behavior rather than from media or social attention.

Overall, the dataset’s impact is best characterized as broad, methodological, and infrastructural: a well-cited climate reference product that has been adopted internationally and used as a common input across multiple STEM subfields concerned with aridity, water balance, and ecological response.
